rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the six-compound elution window while minimizing the risk of missing a strongly retained compound. This establishes the critical pairs and a baseline for subsequent slope and temperature comparisons.
Injection 1 already reached the maximum possible CRF. Shorten the gradient by one grid step to seek a faster fully resolved method while measuring how the critical pair responds to gradient slope.
The 8-minute gradient retained maximum CRF with minimum resolution 3.24, leaving ample margin. Shorten by another grid step to reduce run time while checking that all pairs remain fully resolved.
The critical pair still has resolution 2.46 at a 6-minute gradient. Test a 4-minute gradient, which the slope trend suggests may preserve full resolution while further shortening the separation.

The 4-minute gradient achieves maximum CRF, but its critical pair is close to the resolution threshold. Test higher temperature at the same slope to determine whether thermal selectivity permits a still faster fully resolved separation.

Heating worsened the critical pair, so test the lowest temperature to improve its selectivity while shortening the gradient to the minimum duration. This probes whether cooling can offset the resolution loss from a steeper gradient; injection 4 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method.

Narrowing the gradient reduces its slope enough to potentially lift the critical pair from R 1.23 above 1.5 while retaining the minimum gradient duration. The last peak will likely elute during the final hold, so this tests whether the resolution gain still permits a faster separation than injection 4.

Shift the gradient window upward while preserving the slope that achieved full resolution in injection 7. The stronger final solvent should shorten the last peak’s hold-phase retention; monitor the first pair because its resolution margin is small.

Injection 8 preserved critical-pair resolution when the window shifted upward at constant slope. Shift further to the maximum final organic fraction to accelerate the last peak while testing whether the early pair retains sufficient separation.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step to shorten retention while making the gradient slightly shallower. Check whether the early pair remains resolved as it approaches the weakly retained region; injection 9 is the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method.

Use the critical pair’s improved resolution margin to test a 5 C temperature increase, aiming to shorten the last peak’s retention without losing full resolution. Hold the gradient fixed to isolate the temperature effect.

Test one higher starting-organic step at the temperature most favorable to the critical pair. This probes whether a narrower gradient can shorten the separation further, or whether weak retention of the first two compounds becomes limiting.

Return to the strongest starting solvent that preserved full resolution and test the next temperature step. This brackets the thermal speed limit around injection 11; the critical pair may fall below 1.5, but the maximum-CRF fallback is already established.

Narrow the gradient to recover the critical-pair resolution lost at 35 C while keeping the minimum gradient duration. This tests a warmer, shallower alternative; injection 11 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method.

Shift injection 14’s window downward at the same slope so the first pair experiences more of the gradient rather than eluting near the solvent front. This tests whether better initial retention restores full resolution at 35 C; injection 11 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method.

Refine around injection 11, the fastest confirmed fully resolved method, by reducing the final organic fraction one step. This tests whether a slightly shallower gradient increases the critical-pair resolution margin with only a small retention-time penalty.

Test a lower starting organic fraction near the fastest successful method to keep the first pair farther from the solvent front. The reduced final organic fraction should help preserve resolution, providing another short maximum-CRF candidate with better initial retention.

Cool injection 16 by one temperature step to increase critical-pair resolution while retaining a short separation. Since maximum CRF is already established, this tests a nearby method with greater resolution margin; injection 11 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved option.

Test a short alternative with lower starting organic fraction to retain the first pair farther from the solvent front, while preserving the slope of injection 18. This seeks additional resolution margin at maximum CRF; injection 11 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Raise the final organic fraction from injection 19 to shorten the last peak’s hold-phase retention, using its resolution margin to tolerate the steeper gradient. This refines a fully resolved alternative with better initial retention than injection 11, which remains the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method.

Lower the starting organic fraction one step from injection 9 while retaining the strongest final solvent and minimum gradient duration. This tests whether a fast maximum-CRF method can keep the earliest peaks farther from the solvent front; injection 11 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Reduce the final organic fraction one step from injection 21 to improve its marginal critical-pair resolution while keeping the early peaks well retained. This tests a short maximum-CRF alternative; injection 11 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Test the remaining nearby combination of maximum final solvent strength and modest heating to map the fast-method resolution boundary. This may be marginal for the first pair; injection 11 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method, and the maximum possible CRF is already secured.

Reduce the gradient slope to restore a comfortable resolution margin at 30 C, as the stronger endpoint in injection 23 left the first pair unresolved. This should provide another short maximum-CRF option; injection 11 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Shift the starting organic fraction up one step from injection 24 to shorten retention while retaining a shallower slope than injection 11. This final local refinement should preserve maximum CRF; injection 11 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method at t_last 2.58 min.
